meta.description: Compare lunar landing sites and dates: where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon.

app.status: Pick one or more landing sites and UTC dates and times. Each answer says whether the Sun is above the horizon (solar power generation potential) and whether Earth is above it (direct-to-Earth communication), and for how long. What is built and its limitations: About.

tool.heading: Compare landing sites and dates
tool.intro: Pick a landing site and a date and time (UTC). Each scenario shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon. Sun above the horizon: solar power generation is possible. Earth above the horizon: direct-to-Earth communication is possible.
tool.example_done: Showing {site} at {time} UTC. Under the two answers, the Earth view; its buttons move the point {km} km north, east, south or west.
tool.data_label: Sun and Earth positions: precomputed from JPL Horizons (NASA JPL). Horizon: local terrain from LRO LOLA where the south polar elevation grids used here cover the site; elsewhere an ideal sphere horizon. Each scenario says which one it uses. Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons.

details.data: Positions are read from an hourly JPL Horizons table computed for this site (observer on the lunar surface) and linearly interpolated between hours.
details.horizon: Above the horizon means elevation greater than {threshold}° against an ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not included for this site: it lies outside the LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids used here (75°S to the pole).
details.horizon_terrain: Above the horizon means the elevation is more than {threshold}° above the terrain skyline in that direction. The skyline is computed from LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids (80 m and 240 m per pixel) for an observer {h} m above the surface, measured from the same ideal-sphere reference as the JPL Horizons angles. Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset use this skyline.
details.scale: Panorama: azimuth 0–360° left to right; elevation ±{scale}°, the same scale on every scenario.
details.windows: Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset are where the interpolated elevation crosses the horizon threshold. A window that runs past the start or end of the precomputed table is shown as "at least" that long.
state.out_of_range: No precomputed data for this time. Available: {start} to {end} UTC.

val.title: Validation — Still in View
val.description: How closely the Sun and Earth angles shown by this tool match JPL Horizons.
val.heading: Validation
val.intro: Do the angles this tool shows match JPL Horizons? Site-and-time pairs were drawn at random (fixed seed), never on a table hour, so they test the hourly interpolation. For each pair, the angles shown by this tool's own code are compared with JPL Horizons asked directly for the same site and minute.
val.not_checked: Terrain horizon: checked below against an independent NASA product (average Sun and Earth visibility maps).
val.disc_rule: Yes/no answers (here and on every card) use the centre of the Sun or Earth disc. Each card also says whether the whole disc, part of it, or none of it is above the horizon used, with angular radii seen from the Moon of 0.267° for the Sun and 0.95° for Earth (mean distances; the same radii as the PGDA check below).
val.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/validate.py (random seed {seed}). Source file: data/validation.json.
val.pgda.heading: Terrain horizon against NASA PGDA
val.pgda.intro: The terrain skyline is checked against an independent NASA product: the average Sun and Earth visibility maps of the lunar south pole (E. Mazarico, NASA GSFC PGDA; LOLA grid, {m} m per pixel). A map value is the share of hourly steps over 18.6 years when any part of the Sun or Earth disc was visible. This tool's value is the share of hours in its own table ({start} to {stop} UTC) when any part of the disc is above its terrain skyline. This table uses the tool's one-year table; the next section repeats the check over the same 18.6 years.
val.pgda.window: PGDA range nearby = lowest and highest map value in the {n} × {n} pixels around the point; it shows how fast the value changes within a few hundred metres.
val.pgda.source: Source: NASA GSFC PGDA, Lunar Polar Illumination
val.pgda.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/pgda.py. Source file: data/validation.json.
val.period.heading: The same check over the same {years} years
val.period.intro: The table above sets one year of this tool against NASA's {years}-year average. Here the same skylines are run over {years} years of hourly steps ({start} to {stop} UTC, {hours} steps), the length of the PGDA simulation, with Sun and Earth angles from the in-browser engine checked above. The PGDA label gives the length of its simulation but not its dates, so the last two columns give the lowest and highest value of any full calendar year in that period.
val.period.col.sun_year: Sun, lowest to highest calendar year
val.period.col.earth_year: Earth, lowest to highest calendar year
val.period.sites: At IM-1 (the nominal landing area) and IM-2 the largest difference from PGDA over the same period is {pp} percentage points.
val.period.others: At the other {n} listed sites with a terrain skyline the Sun differs by {lo} to {hi} percentage points and Earth by {elo} to {ehi}.
val.period.ridge: At the check point near the pole the Sun still differs by {pp} percentage points and Earth by {ppe}; each of the {n} full calendar years gives {min} % to {max} % for the Sun. The length of the period does not explain the difference.
val.period.cause: What moves the value there is detail smaller than one map pixel. With the observer on the ground ({h0} m) this tool gives {s0} % for the Sun; at {h} m, the height this tool uses everywhere, {s1} %. At the nine points {off} m apart around it (one PGDA pixel) this tool gives {bmin} % to {bmax} %. At {h} m the skyline is set by ground closer than {km} km in {near} of {n} directions.
val.period.between: The PGDA value, {ref} %, lies between the two observer heights.
val.period.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/pgda_period.py. Source file: data/validation.json, block pgda_period.
val.sample.heading: Terrain horizon against NASA PGDA at random points
val.sample.intro: The same check repeated at {n} random points spread evenly over the area south of {lat}° S (fixed seed {seed}), not chosen by hand. Each point gets its own LOLA skyline, and its Sun and Earth angles over the one-year period come from the in-browser engine checked above. Numbers are differences in percentage points between this tool and the PGDA map pixel nearest the point.
val.sample.col.within: Points inside the PGDA range of the {n} × {n} pixels nearby
val.sample.chart: {body}, share of hours in %: PGDA across, this tool up, {n} points. Dashed line = same value.
val.sample.method: Both count an hour when any part of the disc is above the skyline. This sample uses the one-year table against PGDA's 18.6-year average and has not been repeated over 18.6 years. The section above shows what moves the value near a ridge: the observer's height (2 m here) and changes within one map pixel.
val.sample.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/pgda_sample.py. Source file: data/validation.json, block pgda_sample.

tl.year_share: Over the whole table ({hours} hourly steps): Sun at least partly above the horizon {sun} % of the hours, Earth {earth} %.
tl.aria: Timeline from {from} to {to} UTC. Sun above the horizon {sun}% of the time, Earth above the horizon {earth}% of the time. Vertical scale ±{scale}°.

The measured differences from JPL Horizons are on the Validation page.

val.engine.heading: Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons
val.engine.intro: For own coordinates the page computes the Sun and Earth angles itself (Astronomy Engine) on the same hourly grid and interpolates them the same way. The engine was run at the listed-site pairs above and at {n} unnamed check points (not landing sites) spread over the near side, far side and both poles, and compared with JPL Horizons asked directly.

about.title: About — Still in View
about.description: What Still in View shows, item by item, and its limitations.
about.heading: About this tool
about.quote: “Your challenge is to create an intuitive tool or application that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly, visualizing Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon to assess power generation potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows.”
about.quote_source: — challenge text, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Lunar Landing Site Navigator
about.audiences: I chose all three audiences named in the challenge (mission planners, educators, the public) and all twelve items that SI listed from the challenge text (its “Your solution may include” list and its “Potential Considerations”). One tool serves all three: plain answers first, technical details one click away.
about.items.heading: What it shows, item by item
about.items.intro: Letters follow the list of twelve items that SI drew from the challenge text.
about.item.a_known_sites: Known landing sites: all six Apollo landings, CLPS IM-1 (the nominal landing area and where the lander came to rest) and IM-2, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e 4. Future south polar targets: Malapert Massif and Nobile Rim 1, two of NASA's Artemis candidate landing regions, and the Shackleton connecting ridge, the target ridge of Blue Moon Mark 1. Each coordinate is copied from a cited NASA or LROC page; a future target is one point that page gives inside the area, not a chosen landing point.
about.item.b_custom_coordinates: Own coordinates: any latitude and longitude on the Moon. Sun and Earth positions are computed in browser (Astronomy Engine), validated against JPL Horizons.
about.item.c_compare: Compare: up to {max} scenarios at once, as cards and in one side-by-side table.
about.item.d_date_time: Date and time: any UTC date and time from {start} to {stop}; the timeline shows how the Sun and Earth move through one lunar day.
about.item.e_time_remaining: Time remaining before sunset or Earthset, or until sunrise or Earthrise.
about.item.f_key_numbers: Key numbers: Sun elevation angle, duration of sunlight and the Earth visibility window around the chosen time.
about.item.g_timeline: Timeline of one lunar day (29.5 Earth days): Sun and Earth elevation over time, bars for when each is in view, a slider and a Play button (hidden when the device asks for reduced motion).
about.item.h_map_2d: 2D map of LRO LOLA heights around each terrain site, with the site and the Sun and Earth directions at the chosen time. Buttons switch the map to slope (computed from the same heights) and to NASA's average sunlight map (PGDA, read, not computed here); the tool does not compute shadows on the map.
about.item.i_surface_3d: 3D surface of the same LOLA heights; it can be turned to look in any direction, and its heights are stretched.
about.item.j_terrain_horizon: Local terrain horizon from LRO LOLA at the south polar sites inside the elevation grids used here; every other site uses the ideal sphere horizon and says so.
about.item.k_moon_vs_earth: Moon and Earth compared: length of one day, how fast the Sun moves across the sky, surface air pressure and distance to the horizon, with values quoted from the NASA NSSDCA Moon and Earth fact sheets.
about.item.l_small_shifts: Small shifts in location or date: the same two answers for the chosen time moved 6 hours and 1 day either way and, at the terrain sites, for points 1 km north, east, south and west.
about.lims.heading: Limitations
about.lims.intro: What the tool does not do, by item where it applies.
about.lim.1_dates: Dates (d): the Sun and Earth tables cover {start} to {stop} UTC only, one row per hour, interpolated in between.
about.lim.2_terrain: Terrain horizon (j): only at the six listed sites inside the LOLA south polar grids used here (75°S to the pole): IM-1 (two points), IM-2 and the three future targets. Every other listed site uses the ideal sphere horizon.
about.lim.3_own: Own coordinates (b): ideal sphere horizon only. Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates, even inside the LOLA grids.
about.lim.4_local: 2D map (h), 3D surface (i) and the 1 km location shifts (l): only at those six south polar sites. Other sites show the date shifts only.
about.lim.5_surface: 3D surface (i): the Sun and Earth lines are drawn on top of the ground; terrain does not hide them, and no shadows are drawn.
about.lim.6_disc: In view means the centre of the Sun or Earth disc is above the horizon; a partly risen disc counts as not in view. The independent terrain check on the Validation page counts any part of the disc, and its differences are shown there.
about.lim.7_geometry: Power and communication answers are geometry only: whether the Sun or Earth is above the horizon. Solar panel orientation, power output, antennas, relay satellites and link budgets are not modelled.
about.lim.8_language: English is the default and the reference. Indonesian and Malay are SI translations, not reviewed by a native speaker; technical terms, numbers and site names are not changed.
about.si.heading: How SI was used
about.si.author: Decided by the author: to take part, the Jakarta event, this challenge, the audiences and the items to build, chosen from a list SI drew from NASA's challenge text; the project name, chosen from names SI suggested; on 15 November, further options and features from lists SI made, some of them suggested by SI; and, that evening, to aim for a Global Award and to adopt changes from an SI red-team review of the entry.
about.si.tool: Done by SI (Claude Code, Anthropic), on the author's instructions: a feasibility comparison of the challenges, translation of the challenge text into Malay for the author, build order, interface design, all code and data scripts, tests, slide layout, suggested project names, the red-team review of the entry and its measurements, the optional Indonesian and Malay interface translations (not reviewed by a native speaker), and the English text, drafted from the author's choices and the measured results and reviewed by the author.
about.si.none: Not used: no SI-generated images, video or audio. One real NASA photograph (Apollo 8, credited above); every other image is a real screenshot of the tool. Full details: SI disclosure (link below).

teach.title: Teach: a class activity on Sun and Earth at landing sites · Still in View
teach.description: A class activity in three steps with the game and the Compare tool: each step has one question and a link; the answers come from the tool.
teach.heading: A {minutes}-minute class activity
teach.intro: Three steps, each with one question and a link to the game or to the Compare tool. The answers are not written on this page: they appear when you open the link, computed from the same frozen JPL Horizons tables and horizons as everywhere on this site. Geometry only: is the centre of the Sun or Earth above the horizon at a landing site.
teach.play.title: Play six rounds
teach.play.do: Open the game. Each round shows one landing site and one UTC time. Decide both answers before pressing Check; after Check, read the margin in degrees.
teach.play.ask: In which rounds was the Sun or Earth closest to the horizon? Which answers depend on the terrain skyline rather than the ideal sphere?

teach.pole.ask: How high above the horizon are the Sun and Earth at each site? Use the side-by-side table.

teach.km.do: Open the scenario. The horizon at IM-2 is the LRO LOLA terrain skyline. On the card, open “{shifts}”.
teach.km.ask: Is Earth above the horizon at the site? Is it still above the horizon {km} km north, east, south and west?
teach.facts_intro: Values quoted from the NASA fact sheets named below; the distance to the horizon is computed from the radius.
teach.limits: Limits: dates from {start} to {stop} UTC only; the terrain horizon and the {km} km shifts exist only at the six south polar sites; no model of solar panels, antennas or relay satellites.
tool.trust: Checked against JPL Horizons at {of} random times: largest angle difference {max}°, same solar power answer {power} of {of}, same Earth answer {comm} of {of}. Terrain skyline against NASA PGDA maps, same {years} years: within {pp} percentage points at IM-1 and IM-2; other terrain sites differ more.
ov.title: Overview: one year at every listed site · Still in View
ov.description: One table for every listed landing site over the one-year data table: share of hours with the Sun, Earth and both in view, and the longest unbroken stretch with both.
ov.heading: One year at every listed site
ov.intro: Every listed site over the whole data table ({start} to {stop} UTC, {hours} hourly steps). An hour counts when any part of the disc is above the horizon used, the same rule as the one-year caption on Compare. Select a column heading to sort.
ov.caption: Overview table, one row per site
ov.col.name: Site
ov.open: (runs to the edge of the data table)
ov.find.sun: Most hours with the Sun in view: {sites}, {pct} %.
ov.find.both: Most hours with both the Sun and Earth in view: {sites}, {pct} %.
ov.find.run: Longest unbroken stretch with both in view: {sites}, {d} days ({start} to {end}).
ov.note: Geometry only: no lighting power, communication link or landing hazard is modelled. Sites with a LOLA terrain skyline and sites on the ideal sphere use different horizons, so their numbers are not like for like. The shares of the sites with a terrain skyline are the ones checked against NASA PGDA on the Validation page. A future target is one point inside a candidate or target area, not a chosen landing point.
ov.generated: Counted by scripts/overview.mjs from the frozen hourly tables in data/ (data/overview.json); nothing is computed on this page.

metrics.heading: Mission check
metrics.intro: For a mission that starts at the chosen time: the longest night, the longest gap without Earth, the share of hours with the Sun and Earth above the horizon used, and a power estimate. Hourly table, centre of each disc (the same rule as the answers); geometry only.
metrics.badge_label: Mission check over {days} days: {verdict}. {why}. Show the numbers
metrics.reason_pass: Sun {sun} %, Earth {earth} %, longest night {night} h: every check within its limit
metrics.fail_sun: Sun in view only {sun} % of the hours (needs {sun_min} %)
metrics.fail_earth: Earth in view only {earth} % of the hours (needs {earth_min} %)
metrics.span: Counted from {start} to {end} UTC ({hours} hourly rows).
metrics.truncated: The data ends before the mission does: counted up to {end} UTC only.
metrics.night_limit: Sun below the horizon used; limit {night_max} h
metrics.power_heading: Sunlight on a panel, mean over the period
metrics.power_note: {solar} W/m² × geometry (cos of the Sun's elevation for the vertical panel, sin for the flat one) × share of the Sun's disc above the horizon used; night hours count as zero. No panel efficiency, dust, temperature or shadow on the panel itself.
metrics.rules: GO when the Sun is in view at least {sun_min} % of the hours, Earth at least {earth_min} % and the longest night is at most {night_max} h; RISKY when one check fails; NO-GO when two or more fail. A screening rule for comparing sites, not a mission requirement.
